video_title: Analytics is Winning. But is the Game? | The Stepback with Blake Griffin

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The rise of analytics in sports and its impact on the game
quotes.excerpt: Analytics is everywhere in sports and that's not a bad thing. It can be extremely helpful.
quotes.quote: The year was 1998. Michael Jordan and the Chicago Bulls had just won a sixth NBA title. Mark Maguire and Sammy Sosa were in the middle of a historic home run chase. And most importantly, Will Smith released the music video for Welcome to Miami. It was a year when America looked at moderation and said, no thanks, I'm not a coward. But meanwhile, the small market Oakland Athletics were fighting to compete. And general manager Billy Beane had just hired a Harvard economics graduate named Paul DePodesta. Together, they were about to launch a new way of thinking that wouldn't just change baseball, it would change all sports. Analytics is everywhere in sports and that's not a bad thing. It can be extremely helpful, but it's not everything. It's just knowledge. And it's important to remember knowledge is no replacement for wisdom.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The Oakland Athletics' use of analytics to find undervalued talent
quotes.excerpt: The Oakland A's were basically Laney Boggs in She's All That.
quotes.quote: That might look like just a home run, but in reality, you're seeing the origin of modern analytics. The Oakland A's didn't have more money. They certainly weren't more talented. They were just able to see value that had been overlooked, like in a 90s teen movie when a girl would take off her glasses and become magically hot. What I'm saying is the Oakland A's were basically Laney Boggs in She's All That. But early analytics helped teams be more competitive and made the game more fair. But somewhere along the way, turning numbers into a superpower became shot charts, probability graphs, spin rates, and this.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The evolution of sports scouting from instinct to data-driven optimization
quotes.excerpt: For most of baseball's history, scouting talent wasn't really about numbers. It was about instinct.
quotes.quote: I want to take a step back to look at how analytics evolved into optimization and why we went from searching for overlooked talent to manufacturing complete uniformity. For most of baseball's history, scouting talent wasn't really about numbers. It was about instinct. That's pro scout Mark Baka. And I got to be honest, he sounds like he's got an uncle-level understanding of the game. Listen, there's hitting, there's running, and guys are on a big old field. So the pre-analytics system was a lot of guys like this sitting in the stands wearing vertical stripes looking for the next big thing, ideally someone who excelled in one, maybe two of the five tools.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The 'good face' scouting philosophy in Moneyball
quotes.excerpt: Some of the scouts still believed they could tell by the structure of a young man's face.
quotes.quote: In his famous book Moneyball, Michael Lewis describes an even simpler approach to evaluating a young prospect. Some of the scouts still believed they could tell by the structure of a young man's face not only his character but his future in pro ball. They had a phrase they used: the good face. So imagine working your whole life to get drafted, thousands of hours in the dirt, throwing, hitting, letting your dad yell at you in the batting cages, just to find out you're not hot enough for the big leagues. Kid, listen up. I mean, you hit like a monster, but my god, you got to face a one-two. And what's going on with those eyebrows?

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The New York Yankees' financial advantage and free agent strategy
quotes.excerpt: Rich teams like the Yankees thrived in that system, not because they were better at scouting.
quotes.quote: Rich teams like the Yankees thrived in that system, not because they were better at scouting total hotties, but because they could always attract top free agents with huge contracts. Like when the Yankees had Derek Jeter, an All-Star shortstop, and they went and got Alex Rodriguez, another All-Star shortstop, just to move him to third base, a position he never played. And this is the ultimate rich guy hoarding. Instead of wine or guns from the Civil War, it's infielders.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The impact of Bill James and sabermetrics on baseball
quotes.excerpt: Sabermetrics is the use of stats and data to figure out what actually helps teams win.
quotes.quote: He started reading the work of Bill James, who is referred to as the godfather of sabermetrics. Now, if you don't know about sabermetrics, congrats. You've probably had sex before. Also, nice. Sabermetrics is the use of stats and data to figure out what actually helps teams win. So instead of asking, does he look like a baseball player, and are his lips as soft as they look, or I wonder if he likes me as much as I like him, it became, does he get on base? And baseball nerds started building equations to measure things that had always been there but weren't being valued properly.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The rise of optimization and tech-focused management in the NBA
quotes.excerpt: The rise of the efficiency mindset, looks-maxing, and the mandatory tech-vest.
quotes.quote: We've all seen the rise of the efficiency mindset, looks-maxing, and the mandatory tech-vest. So these vests and analytics moved to basketball, where executives like Daryl Morey helped to bring that same Moneyball thinking into the NBA, prioritizing efficiency above everything else. Morey completely changed how the Rockets would play basketball for decades, because the math was clear. Three-pointers were way more worth the attempt than a two-pointer.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The negative consequences of copying analytics without proper personnel
quotes.excerpt: Everyone copied the math without having the same personnel. What started as innovation became imitation.
quotes.quote: The problem is everyone copied the math without having the same personnel. What started as innovation became imitation, like crab with a K, or the Fabio butter, or Morkey Mouse. And once every team is chasing the same optimal shots, you don't get smarter basketball, you just get this. The Hornets and the Bulls combined to shoot 22 for 97 from three-point range on Friday. They missed 75 three-pointers. I couldn't turn it off.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The Houston Rockets' record-breaking missed three-pointers in 2018
quotes.excerpt: On May 28, 2018, during Game 7 of the Western Conference Finals, a team set the record.
quotes.quote: On May 28, 2018, during Game 7 of the Western Conference Finals, a team set the record for most consecutive missed threes. Yes, obviously, it was Daryl Morey's Houston Rockets. And when do you stop shooting is a great question, and the answer is when you lose. Afterwards, Morey would tell ESPN's Tim MacMahon, quote, we should have won tonight. I don't have much else to say. And it turns out when you miss 27 three-pointers, not having much else to say is actually your 28th miss of the night.

quotes.summary_phrase: Dave Roberts' decision-making in the 2025 World Series

Then in the 11th inning, Will Smith, no, not that Will Smith, this Will Smith, hit a home run to win the World Series. He'd been 0 for 4 in the game. Statistically, he should have been pulled for a pinch hitter.

quotes.speaker: Blake Griffin
quotes.summary_phrase: The importance of human elements in sports beyond analytics
quotes.excerpt: No one is saying to get rid of analytics. We should use all the information we have.
quotes.quote: No one is saying to get rid of analytics. We should use all the information we have. But we do need to stop treating optimization like it's the entire point of sports. Take it from Art Howe, the manager of the A's during the Moneyball era.

text_blocks.speaker: Art Howe
text_blocks.text: I believe in people more than numbers. You know, and the analytics to me, no two games are the same and depending and no two situations are the same. But to say that put a blanket, say this is the way you should do it every time, I don't agree with that. I never did, never will, because the human factor is involved.
